## Survey error

## Total Survey Error

![](images/lifecycle.png){fig-align="center" width="30%"}

From [@groves2009survey]

::: notes
-   In previous classes we've mostly dealt with the kinds of errors that come from the left branch of the diagram: errors that come from the measurement process. In the next classes, we'll focus more on the RHS: errors that result from the process of attempting to represent a target population using (typically) less than the total number of people.
:::

## Total Survey error

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Errors of representation appear when there is some difference between who we end up measuring and who we want to measure.

-   The [target population]{.yellow} is some finite set of observations we want to know something about.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/lifecycle_rhs.png){fig-align="center" width="30%"}
:::
:::::

## Target Populations

-   The American National Election Study targets U.S. citizens age 18 or older living in the 48 contiguous states of the U.S. or Washington, D.C. during a period prior to or just after a U.S. presidential election.

-   National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey targets the non-institutionalized civilian resident population of the U.S. in a given year.

-   The Youth Risk Behavior Survey targets public and private school students in grades 9-12 in the United States in a given year.

## Surveying the whole population

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   The U.S. Census try to measure the entire population of interest.

-   Obviously this is not practical for most surveys that seek to measure something about the U.S. population.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/census-logo-sharing-card.jpg)
:::
:::::

::: notes
While its rare to do this when sampling *people*, its not uncommon for other kinds of research to work with entire populations: people who study members of congress, for instance, are typically working with data on all the current members.

(This leads to some conceptual awkwardness, because a lot of important concepts in statistical inference assume we're working with a sample)
:::

## Not surveying the whole population

-   More often, surveys will attempt to measure some sample of the target population.

-   The hope is that the sampled units are representative of the target population, but to the extent they're not, this introduces new sources of error.

::: notes
Working with samples means we need to understand individual estimates as realizations of a repeatable process.
:::

## Sampling Frames

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   A [sampling frame]{.yellow} is the list of elements in the target population
-   A list of elements isn't always available: we might have a list of phone numbers, but not "all adults in the U.S."
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/Auckland_Yellow_pages.jpg)
:::
:::::

## Sampling Frames and coverage error

[coverage error]{.yellow} results from differences between the sampling frame and the target population.

-   For example: we might want to measure all U.S. citizens, but our list of phone numbers leaves out unlisted numbers and people without phones.

-   Random digit dialing gives a way around the first problem, but not the second.

## Sampling Error

[Sampling error]{.yellow} is the gap between the sampling frame and the sample.

-   This is always present when we sample, but under the right conditions, we can say a lot about the likelihood of an error of a given size.

## Sampling Distributions

The [sampling distribution]{.yellow} is the distribution of sample statistics across *all possible realizations of a sample.*

## Sampling Distribution: example

Imagine we've got test scores for 8 students:

$$
72, 74, 76, 77, 81, 84, 85, 91
$$

::: fragment
The sampling distribution for a sample of size 10 from this "population" would just be every possible combination of 2 values: $[72, 74], [72, 76], [72, 77]...$
:::

## Sampling Distribution: example

```{r, echo=TRUE}
data<-c(72, 74, 76, 77, 81, 84, 85, 91)
# all possible samples of size 2:
combn(data, 2)

```

## Sampling distribution: the central limit theorem

-   Again, this isn't something we typically know. If we knew the population values, we wouldn't draw a sample in the first place.

-   However, because of the central limit theorem, we *do* know some things about the sampling distributions of means and proportions.

## Sampling distribution: CLT

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: smaller
-   The sampling distribution of the mean will be normally distributed.
-   The mean of the sampling distribution will equal the population mean.
-   The variance of the sampling distribution will equal $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}

## Sampling variance: CLT

::: smaller
-   The sampling variance of the sample mean is: $$v(\bar{y}) = \frac{\sum^n_{i=1}(y_i - \bar{y})}{n-1} $$

-   The sampling variance for a proportion would be: $$\frac{p(1-p)}{n}$$

-   The standard error of the mean is just the square root of this sampling variance. $s(\bar{y}) = \sqrt{v(\bar{y})}$
:::

## Sampling distribution: CLT

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
This is important because the mean and variance are all we really need to know about a normal distribution to know the probability of generating a particular value.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/norm_colored.png)
:::
:::::

## Sampling distribution: CLT

The CLT is how we know the margin of error for a survey statistic: its the range that would contain 95% of sampled proportions in the sampling distribution.

![](images/norm.png){fig-align="center" width="30%"}

## Sampling distribution: CLT

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

$$.48 (1-.48) \approx .25$$

::: fragment

$$\sqrt{\frac{2.5}{1000}} = 0.005$$


:::

::: fragment


$$ .005 \times 1.96 \approx 0.031 = 3.1\% $$
:::

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/241011-election-poll-3x2-4c78ec.webp)
:::
:::::

## Sampling distribution: CLT

-   One key challenge here, is that the Central Limit Theorem assumes simple random sampling with replacement, but this isn't what we typically have in survey data.

-   Accounting for these differences adds some additional complexity.

## Sample designs

### Simple random samples

-   In simple random samples, all elements have an equal probability of being selected.

-   This is the simplest method, but its also exceedingly rare in surveys because its inefficient.

::: notes
SRS is the easiest to understand and methodologically the easiest to work with.

But its wildly inefficient for most applications.
:::

## Cluster-sampling

-   In a cluster sample, "groups" of observations are sampled instead of sampling each individual.

-   For instance: a survey of students might randomly select 50 classes and then interview all students in those classes.

::: notes
This is partly a cost-saving measure. It's much easier to create a sampling frame for "all city blocks" or "all classrooms" than to create one for "all people". Moreover, its more efficient because the selected units are close to each other.
:::

### Cluster-sampling

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   Imagine you're gauging support for an upcoming referendum.
-   You sample 2 city blocks to get an $n=100$
-   (The population mean here is 50)
:::

### Cluster-sampling: design effects

Since we're dealing with proportions, the variance under a simple random sample is just: $\frac{p(1-p)}{n}$

. . .

So, the variance under SRS is: $\frac{.5(1-.5)}{100} = 0.0025$

. . .

The sampling variance for the clustered samples is $\approx 0.03$, so the clustering increases the variance by $0.03/0.0025 = 12$

### Cluster-sampling: design effects

-   This ratio of the clustered variance relative to the estimate is called the [design effect]{.yellow} or $d^2$.

-   Note that the $d^2$ will depend on what you're estimating and will increase or decrease depending on the amount of homogeneity within clusters with respect to the thing you're estimating.

## Stratification

### Stratification

-   [Strata]{.yellow} are *mutually exclusive* and *collectively exhaustive* subsets of the population.

-   Stratified Sampling means separating the elements into strata and then drawing a sample from each one.

### Stratification

### Stratification

Stratification can *reduce* sampling variance because it limits the chance of drawing highly non-representative samples.

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   For instance, the ANES stratifies counties/metro areas based on vote share, turnout, and region
-   This ensures that there are no potential random samples that entirely exclude very Republican or very Democratic counties.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/anes_sample_method.png)
:::
:::::


### Stratification

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Think back to the example of drawing samples of n=2 from 8 student test scores
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

![](images/student_scores1.png){fig-align="center" width="15%"}
:::
:::::

::::: {.columns}

### Stratification

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
The "worst" samples are no longer possible here: because my sample always contains at least some "high" and some "low" scorers.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/stratified_table.png){fig-align="center" width="37%"}

:::
:::::


### Stratification

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Sampling variance under SRS: $16$
- Sampling variance under stratification: $4.5$
- Design effect: $.28$
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
data<-data.frame( data=   c(72, 74, 76, 77, 81, 84, 85, 91),
                  strata = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2)
                   )



combos<-combn(seq(nrow(data)), 2)
cb<-apply(combos, 1, function(x) data[x,])|>dplyr::bind_cols()
colnames(cb)<-c('obs1', 'strata1', 'obs2', 'strata2' )
rownames(cb)<-NULL
cb<-cb[,c(1, 3, 2, 4)]
cb$`Possible with stratified sample?`<- factor(apply(cb[,c(3,4)], 1, function(x) length(unique(x))), labels=c("No", "Yes"))
cb$means<-rowMeans(cb[,1:2])
cb$sample<-'SRS'

bind_rows(cb, cb|>filter(`Possible with stratified sample?` == "Yes")|>mutate(sample="Stratified"))|>
  ggplot(aes(x=means, fill=sample) )  + geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, color='black') +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x='Sample means')+
  facet_wrap(~sample, ncol=1) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

:::
:::::


### Stratification: requirements

- Note that stratification assumes I already have the stratification variables before I conduct the survey.

- The benefits of stratification are largest when my stratifying variable is correlated with the stuff I want to estimate (which is why the ANES stratifies on things like regional partisanship and turnout)


### Stratification: proportional allocation to strata

- Under proportional allocation to strata, the number of units selected from each strata is proportional to the size of the strata in the population. 

- These designs are considered "self-weighting": they're already representative of the population.

### Stratification: disproportionate allocation

- Under some conditions, disproportionate allocation may further reduce sampling variance, although this is risky.

- Disproportionate allocation can make it more feasible to study certain subgroups: if I want to get reliable estimates of the views of Alaskans (.2% of the population), I'd otherwise need a huge sample.

### Stratification: disproportionate allocation

- Under disproportionate allocation to strata, strata means must be re-weighted to account for over-representation of certain groups.

- For example: if strata A is $12\%$ of the population but $24\%$ of the sample, then each individual respondent in strata A would be given a weight of $12/24 = .5$




::: notes
Critical detail: stratification, when performed correctly, *reduces* sampling variance.
:::



### Multi-stage sampling

Multi-stage sampling is when population units can be divided into clusters and multiple stages of sampling are required

- For the first stage, a sample is drawn from the clusters: Primary Sampling Units (PSUs).

- For the second stage, a sample is drawn from the units within the sampled clusters: Secondary Sampling Units (SSUs).

### Multi-stage sampling

Examples:

- Select 100s school randomly in MD, sample randomly in each
school.
- Stage 1 = Census blocks, Stage 2 = households


### Finite population corrections

-   Survey samples are typically drawn without replacement, meaning that no element should be sampled more than once.

-   When the sample is only a small share of the population, the effect of this is trivial, but it can influence estimates when the sampling fraction is large. 

### Finite population corrections

The finite population correction adjusts the estimated variance to account for this: 

$$v(\bar{y}) = \frac{1-f}{n} s^2$$

where $f$ is the fraction of the population that was sampled. 

::: fragment

For most surveys, $f$ miniscule, so this doesn't matter much! 

:::


## Response rates

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

- Stratification isn't the only thing we need to account for. 

- Even where our sampling strategy is perfect, issues like differential non-response pose major problems for representativeness. 

- Weighting offers some (imperfect) methods to mitigate this as well.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/response_rates.webp)

:::
:::::




### Snowball Samples

- Snowball samples are a common way to survey hard-to-reach populations or groups: people involved in organized crime, people without a permanent address, trans youth etc.

- They work like a chain letter, where a small number of respondents are identified, and then asked to recommend others who are also part of the sampling frame. 

::: fragment

For small, densely connected communities, a snowball sample may allow researchers to get something approaching the full population.

:::


::: notes
Robert Benford and David Snow used snowball sampling to collect data on homeless advocacy organizations in a selection of cities. It's entirely plausible that a method like this could retrieve every homeless advocacy org in an area.
:::

### Convenience Samples

- The survey for this class is best described as a convenience sample. We're not really making any effort to retrieve a representative sample of the population.

- This means we can't really generalize the results to the population, but convenience samples can still be useful, especially for something like piloting a survey.


::: notes
The survey for this class is best described as a convenience sample. They're commonly used for pilots.
:::
